issues.legal_issue: A tenant who voluntarily gives up possession, whether through a valid surrender or by leaving the land voluntarily, has not been dispossessed for the purpose of claiming restoration under the tenant-protection provision.
material_facts: The tenant held the land under a registered lease and was found to have possessed it during the relevant period.
The High Court found that the tenant surrendered possession before the relevant cutoff, relying on a later revenue-record entry; the Tribunal also found that possession had been surrendered.
The Tribunal considered the surrender invalid because it was not in writing, but even on that assumption the tenant had left possession voluntarily.
There was no finding that the tenant was ousted by legal process or excluded from the land by a physical act.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not dispossessed within the meaning of Section 32(1-B), so he did not satisfy its dispossession requirement and did not become a purchaser under that provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(1-B) requires dispossession, not merely absence from possession. The Court construed “dispossessed” in its ordinary sense, referring to being ousted by legal process or excluded from land by a physical act, consistent with the definition in Black’s Law Dictionary. Voluntarily surrendering possession or leaving it voluntarily is not dispossession, whether or not the surrender is legally valid. The Court also noted the 1956 amendment requiring surrender to be in writing, but held that even an invalid surrender or voluntary departure did not meet the statutory requirement.

predicates.tenant_restoration_claim: A tenant seeks restoration of land under a statutory tenant-protection scheme.
predicates.possession_ended_by_voluntary_departure: The tenant gave up possession by surrendering it or leaving voluntarily.
predicates.tenant_excluded_by_legal_process_or_phys: The tenant was ousted through legal process or excluded from the land by a physical act.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeking statutory restoration gives up possession voluntarily and is not legally or physically excluded, the required dispossession is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A qualifying tenant’s entitlement under the restoration scheme is not defeated merely because the tenant, rather than the landlord, is in possession of the land on the scheme’s specified reference date.
material_facts: The statutory scheme provided for restoration to tenants who had possessed the land on the relevant appointed day and were dispossessed before the specified cutoff, where the land was held by the landlord on a later reference date.
The provision was part of a series of amendments extending purchase and restoration rights to tenants, including tenants evicted before the tillers’ date.
The Court regarded the legislation as beneficial and aimed at enabling tenants who satisfied its conditions to become purchasers of the land.

The Court addressed the situation of a qualifying tenant who was in possession on the later reference date as a matter of statutory construction; the tenant in this appeal was found not to satisfy the separate dispossession requirement.
issues.conclusion: The provision should be read so that a qualifying tenant’s entitlement is not defeated solely because the tenant is in possession on the reference date; the tenant is not to be denied the benefit or made liable to eviction on that ground alone.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(1-B), read in light of its restoration mechanism and the beneficial objective of the Act, should be construed to give effect to the legislature’s intention to confer purchase rights on tenants who satisfy the provision’s conditions. The Court relied on the legislative development of Section 32, including subsections (1), (1-A), and (1-B), and rejected a narrow reading that would give a qualifying tenant who was out of possession greater protection than one who was in possession. No earlier judicial decisions were relied on for this construction.

rule.if: tenant_restoration_proceeding and tenant_had_required_starting_possession and tenant_was_dispossessed_before_relevant_cutoff and tenant_is_in_possession_on_reference_date

predicates.tenant_restoration_proceeding: A tenant seeks the statutory restoration and purchase benefit for agricultural land.
predicates.tenant_had_required_starting_possession: The tenant possessed the land at the starting point required by the restoration scheme.
predicates.tenant_was_dispossessed_before_relevant_: The tenant was dispossessed before the scheme’s relevant cutoff.
predicates.tenant_is_in_possession_on_reference_dat: The tenant, rather than the landlord, possesses the land on the scheme’s later reference date.

issues.definition: A tenant who had the required starting possession and was dispossessed before the relevant cutoff does not lose the statutory benefit solely because the tenant possesses the land on the later reference date.
